segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Come, I will show you the judgment on the great prostitute who sits on many waters,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality, and those who live on the earth became drunk on the wine of her prostitution.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her prostitution,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: “Babylon the Great, the mother of prostitutes and of the abominations of the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the woman drunk on the blood of the holy ones and on the blood of the witnesses of Jesus. When I saw her, I was utterly amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the angel said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Why are you amazed? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, the one with the seven heads and the ten horns.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss, and it goes to destruction. And those who live on the earth, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will be amazed when they see that the beast was, and is not, and will come.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: This calls for a mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. They are also seven kings:

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain for a little while.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: As for the beast that was and is not, it is itself an eighth, and it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received kingship, but they receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: These have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: These will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples and crowds and nations and languages.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the ten horns that you saw, and the beast, these will hate the prostitute and will make her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her up with fire,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, and to act with one purpose and give their kingship to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the woman that you saw is the great city that holds kingship over the kings of the earth.”

notes.phrase: the great prostitute who sits on many waters
notes.note: The Hebrew prophets pictured great cities as prostitutes: Tyre in Isaiah 23, Nineveh in Nahum 3, and Jerusalem itself in Ezekiel 16 and 23. The phrase ‘on many waters’ echoes Jeremiah 51:13, addressed to historical Babylon with its river and canals. A reader steeped in the Greek Old Testament would have heard a city being described before the angel says so in verse 18.

The Greek noun covers unlawful sexual activity in general and is traditionally rendered ‘fornication’ or ‘sexual immorality’. It shares a root with the word for ‘prostitute’ and is here the conduct of a figure so named, so it is rendered ‘prostitution’; the verb translated ‘committed sexual immorality’ is from the same root. In the prophets this imagery stands for idolatry and corrupting alliances, and most interpreters read it that way here.

The Greek has no article and could mean either ‘in the Spirit’ (carried by God’s Spirit) or ‘in spirit’ (in a visionary state rather than bodily). The same phrase marks the major vision scenes of the book (1:10, 4:2, 21:10). Most translations capitalize, as here, but the two senses are not far apart.

The word can be read as part of the inscribed name (‘Mystery, Babylon the Great’, as in the King James Version) or as a comment that the name has a hidden meaning. Most modern translations take the second view, as here, since the angel goes on to explain ‘the mystery of the woman’ in verse 7. In the usage of the period the word means a secret now being disclosed, not an unsolvable puzzle.

Traditionally ‘saints’, which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God’s people’.

The Greek word means ‘witness’, one who testifies; the English word ‘martyr’ derives from it. Many translations use ‘martyrs’ here because these witnesses have been killed. Whether the word had already acquired the technical sense ‘one who dies for the faith’ when Revelation was written is disputed, so the ordinary meaning is kept.

The description parodies the title given to God earlier in the book, ‘the one who is and who was and who is coming’ (1:4, 1:8, 4:8). The beast imitates this, but its middle term is ‘is not’ and its end is destruction. Many scholars also see an allusion to the widespread rumour that Nero would return after his death, though this is not certain.

The Greek word covers both mountains and hills. Rome was known throughout the ancient world as the city on seven hills, and most scholars think first readers would have recognized Rome at once, with ‘Babylon’ as its cipher. Some interpreters instead identify the city as Jerusalem or as a symbol of oppressive worldly power in general.

notes.phrase: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come
notes.note: The identity of the seven kings is disputed. Some match them to particular Roman emperors, though there is no agreement on where to begin counting or whom to include; others take them as successive empires. Others again read seven as a symbolic number for the full span of hostile rule. The text does not settle the question.

The Greek is literally ‘is of the seven’. It may mean that the eighth is one of the seven returning, or that it comes from the seven and shares their character without being one of them. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

The traditional rendering is ‘kingdom’ in verses 12 and 17 and ‘reigns’ or ‘has dominion’ in verse 18. Here the word means not a territory but royal rule itself, the status and power of a king, and one English word is used for all three occurrences. This also keeps the play in verse 18 between ‘kingship’ and ‘kings’.

The same Greek word is rendered ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in this translation where it refers to the non-Jewish peoples as a group. Here it stands in a fourfold list describing the population of the whole world, a formula that recurs throughout Revelation, so ‘nations’ is used.
